items.title: L7: When keywords mislead you about the Behaviour
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A common trap is to match a story to a Behaviour because of a word in it rather than because of what the person did. A story that mentions 'the team' is not automatically Working Together, and a story that mentions a 'deadline' is not automatically Delivering at Pace. Read for the thing that carried the story, not the vocabulary around it. Three checks help. First, find the decision point: what did the person do at the moment things could have gone wrong, and why? Second, find the verb that does the work. Verbs such as 'persuaded', 'explained' and 'listened' point towards Communicating and Influencing; 'compared', 'weighed' and 'chose' point towards Making Effective Decisions; 'trialled', 'suggested' and 'redesigned' point towards Changing and Improving; 'checked', 'corrected' and 'followed up' point towards Managing a Quality Service. Third, ask what the assessor would give credit for if the Behaviour name were hidden. Consider: 'Our team had a deadline on Friday. I worked out which forms would take longest, started those first, and moved two simple ones to a colleague with spare time.' The word 'team' appears, but the credit is for planning and prioritising, so the Behaviour is Delivering at Pace. Likewise, a long story about a customer who was upset may be about Managing a Quality Service if the person's actions were about putting right an error, and not about Communicating and Influencing, even though they spoke to the customer. Keep asking which action earned the credit.

questions.prompt: 'Our team had a deadline on Friday. I worked out which forms would take longest, started those first and passed two simple ones to a colleague with spare time.' Which Behaviour earns the credit?

options.text: Working Together
Leadership
Managing a Quality Service
Delivering at Pace

questions.hint: The credit is for planning and prioritising to a date.

questions.prompt: Why is a story that mentions 'the team' not automatically a Working Together story?

options.text: Working Together stories may not contain the word team, as it is reserved for Leadership
Assessors disregard any group setting and score only individual tasks
The word team signals Working Together only at EO level and above
The vocabulary may surround an action that earns credit under another Behaviour

questions.hint: Credit follows the action, not the word.

questions.prompt: Which verb most strongly points towards Making Effective Decisions?

options.text: Persuaded
Trialled
Weighed
Followed up

questions.hint: Weighing options is the core of decision-making.

questions.prompt: Which verb most strongly points towards Changing and Improving?

options.text: Compared
Listened
Corrected
Trialled

questions.hint: Trying a new approach signals improvement.

questions.prompt: A person speaks to an upset customer, then spends the rest of the story finding and correcting a payment error. Where is the credit mainly earned?

options.text: Communicating and Influencing, because she spoke to the customer
Working Together, because two people were involved
Leadership, because she took charge
Managing a Quality Service, through putting the error right

questions.hint: The actions that earn credit are about correcting the error.

questions.prompt: What is the third check suggested for choosing a Behaviour?

options.text: Count how many times each Behaviour's key word appears in the story
Pick whichever Behaviour is listed first in the advert, as it carries most weight
Choose the Behaviour that has the shortest description in the framework
Ask what the assessor would give credit for if the Behaviour name were hidden

questions.prompt: Which phrase is the best clue to Communicating and Influencing?

options.text: 'I made a list of everything that needed doing and put the urgent items first.'
'I corrected the figures twice before the report was sent to the customer.'
'I explained the change to each group in the words that suited them.'
'I tried a different order for the daily checks and compared the results.'

questions.hint: Adapting an explanation to audiences is the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: A candidate writes 'I was under a lot of pressure to get everything done on time' and then describes how she checked every entry twice. Which Behaviour does the Action show?

options.text: Delivering at Pace
Seeing the Big Picture
Developing Self and Others
Managing a Quality Service

questions.hint: The action is about accuracy, not planning to a date.

questions.prompt: Which is the decision point in this story: 'I noticed two bookings clashed. I phoned both groups, offered each a different slot and agreed the swap by the end of the day'?

options.text: Phoning both groups and offering each an alternative slot
Noticing that two bookings clashed in the diary
Agreeing the swap with both groups by the end of the day
Writing the new date in the booking book once it was settled

questions.hint: The key action at the moment of risk carries the credit.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to pick a Behaviour solely because the story is dramatic?

options.text: Assessors do not accept stories involving upset customers or conflict
The drama is not what is scored; the candidate's actions and reasoning are
Emotional language in an application is marked down at the sift stage
Dramatic stories are nearly always too long for the word limit

questions.hint: The Behaviour is judged on actions.

questions.prompt: Which question helps most when a story seems to fit two Behaviours equally?

options.text: Which of the two could I give the more specific evidence for?
Which of the two Behaviours comes first in the published framework?
Which of the two sounds more senior when read aloud?
Which of the two did my last line manager mention in my appraisal?

questions.hint: Choose the Behaviour with the richer evidence.

items.title: L7: Diagnosing a weak STAR draft
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: When a STAR answer scores poorly the cause is usually one of a small number of faults, and spotting which one lets you fix the draft in minutes. The first fault is a bloated Situation: more than a quarter of the words are spent on background, so the Action is squeezed. The second is a missing or vague Task, so the assessor cannot tell what the candidate was personally responsible for. The third is an Action that is a list of generalities such as 'I communicated with everyone' or that uses 'we' throughout. The fourth is a Result that states a feeling or nothing at all. The fifth is a story that fits a different Behaviour from the one asked about. Consider a draft for Delivering at Pace: 'The charity I volunteer at is a well-known local organisation with many branches. We had a lot of letters to send before the end of the month and everyone worked hard. We got them all out and the manager was happy.' The Situation is wordy, the Task is missing, the Action is entirely 'we' and gives no sign of planning, and the Result is only the manager's mood. The best single repair is to add a specific first-person Action showing how the writer organised the work, because the Action carries the most marks. Candidates often add a number to the Result first, but a number attached to an empty Action cannot save it. Fix the part that carries most credit before polishing the rest.

questions.prompt: In the charity letters draft, which repair would raise the score most?

options.text: Adding a longer description of the charity's history and where its branches are
Adding the name of the manager who was happy with the result
Adding a closing sentence that thanks the assessor for reading the answer
Adding a first-person Action showing how the writer planned and sorted the work

questions.hint: The Action carries the most marks.

questions.prompt: What is the main fault of the sentence 'The charity I volunteer at is a well-known local organisation with many branches'?

options.text: It uses a tense that makes the story sound as if it has not finished
It contains a claim about the charity that the assessor cannot check
It spends words on background that the Action needs
It names the organisation, which is not allowed in a Civil Service application

questions.hint: A bloated Situation squeezes the Action.

questions.prompt: Why does 'We got them all out and the manager was happy' make a weak Result?

options.text: It credits the manager rather than the candidate, which assessors cannot accept
It gives only a mood, with no measure of what changed
It is too short for the assessor to treat as accurate
It uses the word 'all', which counts as an exaggeration

questions.hint: A Result needs outcome and evidence.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely effect of using 'we' throughout an Action?

options.text: The assessor credits the teamwork automatically, so the answer scores well
The assessor cannot tell what the candidate personally did
The answer is marked down for style only, not for evidence
The answer looks more senior, because leaders often say we

questions.prompt: Which fault is shown by 'I communicated with everyone'?

options.text: A Result that has been left out of the answer entirely
A Situation that is missing from the opening of the answer
A general Action that says nothing about how or what was done
A Task that takes up too many of the available words

questions.prompt: A candidate has a precise number in the Result but 'dealt with it' as the whole Action. What is the best advice?

options.text: Keep the Action as it is and add a second, more impressive number to the Result
Remove the Result and use the freed words to expand the Situation
Replace 'dealt with it' with specific steps and reasons, then keep the number
Rewrite the whole answer so it fits a different Behaviour

questions.hint: A number cannot rescue an empty Action.

questions.prompt: What does a missing Task usually leave the assessor unable to judge?

options.text: What the candidate was personally responsible for
In which year and in which month the events took place, with exact dates
How large the organisation was
How the story ended for the customer

questions.prompt: Roughly how large a share of the words should the Situation take before it becomes a problem?

options.text: Anything over ten words
More than about a half
More than about a quarter
Any amount, provided the Action is accurate

questions.prompt: A story is well written and detailed but shows Managing a Quality Service when the question asked about Changing and Improving. What is the fault?

options.text: The Result has been left out of the answer
The Situation takes up too much of the word count
The story fits a different Behaviour from the one asked about
The Task is unclear about who was responsible

questions.prompt: After fixing the Action, which part is usually most worth strengthening next?

options.text: The first sentence, so that it sounds enthusiastic
The final sentence, so that it thanks the assessor
The title of the organisation, so that it is exact
The Result, with an outcome and its evidence

questions.hint: The Result is the next most important element.

items.title: L7: Seeing the Big Picture beyond your desk
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Seeing the Big Picture is often shown badly because candidates describe their own task and add a sentence about 'helping the department'. Stronger evidence shows how understanding of the wider purpose changed what the person did. Three layers are worth knowing. The first is the team's purpose: why the team exists and who depends on its work. The second is the department's aims, usually found in publicly available documents such as a department's published plan or objectives. The third is the public and the wider context: how decisions affect real people, other organisations and sometimes costs to the taxpayer. At AO level the expectation is mainly the first layer and awareness of the second. Take an officer who processes applications. She notices that a particular error stops the application being passed on to another team, which then phones the customer, who is then delayed and calls again. She realises that fixing the error at her desk avoids three further contacts. She changes her checking order and tells her supervisor what she found. The evidence is the connection she makes, the action she takes because of it, and the result. A weak version would say 'I know my work supports the department's goals' without any change in behaviour. Note that Seeing the Big Picture does not require you to know policy in detail, but it does require you to understand why your work matters and to adjust your own choices because of it.

questions.prompt: An officer realises that an error at her desk causes another team to phone the customer, who then calls again. She changes her checking order. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Changing and Improving
Seeing the Big Picture
Managing a Quality Service
Communicating and Influencing

questions.hint: She links her work to wider effects and acts on it.

questions.prompt: Which is the best evidence that understanding of the wider purpose changed behaviour?

options.text: 'I am aware that my work supports the department's goals in many ways.'
'I always try to see the larger picture in everything I do.'
'My team has a clear mission statement displayed on the wall.'
'Knowing the payment covered a family's rent, I did those cases first.'

questions.hint: A change in action shows the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: At AO level, which layers of the big picture are mainly expected?

options.text: The team's purpose, with awareness of the department's aims
Government-wide strategy across all departments
International treaties and how they affect the department
The annual budgets of the whole Civil Service

questions.hint: Entry level is mostly the immediate team and department.

questions.prompt: Where could a candidate find the department's aims in order to prepare?

options.text: Social media posts written by staff in the department
Newspaper opinion columns about the department
Its published plan or objectives on GOV.UK
A telephone directory of the department's offices

questions.hint: Public departmental documents are the source.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I know my work supports the department's goals' weak?

options.text: It is too long to be read within the word limit
It is a claim, with no example of how it changed what she did
Departments do not publish goals that applicants can refer to
It names the wrong layer of the big picture for an AO role

questions.prompt: Which action most clearly shows seeing the wider impact of a delay?

options.text: Prioritising cases where a delay would stop a payment reaching a household
Working through the cases in the alphabetical order of the customers' surnames
Asking a colleague to sort the post before starting
Answering the phone before replying to any emails

questions.hint: Impact on the public drives the choice.

questions.prompt: Does Seeing the Big Picture require detailed knowledge of policy?

options.text: Not detailed policy, but understanding why the work matters and acting on it
Detailed policy knowledge, which is essential at every grade
Detailed policy knowledge, but only for EO and above
Neither, because the Behaviour concerns only the size of the team

questions.hint: The Behaviour is about purpose and its effect on choices.

questions.prompt: After finding the error at her desk, what should the officer do besides changing her own checks?

options.text: Say nothing, to avoid drawing attention to the error
Tell her supervisor what she found, so others can benefit
Wait for the other team to complain before acting
Ask the customer to check the form in future

questions.hint: Sharing the finding widens the benefit.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a strong Result for the officer's story?

options.text: She felt more confident about her work and about her role in the wider department as a result
Repeat calls on those cases fell, and the other team stopped receiving incomplete forms
Her supervisor was pleased with what she had done
She enjoyed learning about how the department fits together

questions.hint: A Result shows effect on the wider process.

questions.prompt: The third layer of the big picture refers to which of these?

options.text: The physical layout of the building the team works in
The size of the team and its reporting line
The software the team uses for processing
The effect on the public, other organisations and costs

items.title: L7: Making a decision with incomplete information
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Real decisions at work are rarely made with all the facts. The Behaviour Making Effective Decisions does not ask for certainty; it asks for sensible judgement about what you know, what you do not, and what to do next. A useful sequence is: define the decision, gather what can be gathered in the time available, identify the risks of acting and of waiting, take advice where it is available, decide, record the reasoning and review the outcome. Consider a clerk who finds a form with a missing signature on the last day before a payment cut-off. She cannot reach the customer. The options are to process it anyway, to reject it, or to hold it and flag it. She checks the guidance, finds that a missing signature makes a form invalid, and weighs the risk of delaying a payment against the risk of paying on an invalid form. She asks her team leader, who confirms the guidance, so she holds the form, arranges a letter with a clear explanation and records the reason. The decision is sound even though the outcome, a delay, is not what the customer wanted. A good answer shows that she understood the rules, the risk of each choice and when to ask for advice. A weak answer would say 'I decided to process it because the customer needed the money', which shows sympathy but no regard for the rule. Another weak answer would say 'I left it for my manager' without having weighed anything. Good decisions can still have unwelcome outcomes, so explain your reasoning, not just the result.

questions.prompt: A clerk finds an unsigned form on the last day before a payment cut-off. Which course shows the best judgement?

options.text: Process it anyway, so that the customer is not left without money over the cut-off
Throw the form away and hope the customer sends another one
Leave it where it is for a colleague to find on the next shift
Check the guidance, ask her team leader, hold the form and write to the customer

questions.hint: She followed the rule, took advice and explained.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I processed it because the customer needed the money' a weak decision answer?

options.text: It shows sympathy but no weighing of the rule or the risk
Customers rarely need payments by a particular date
The decision was taken too quickly to be recorded
It makes no mention of consulting a colleague

questions.hint: Reasoning must include rules and risks.

questions.prompt: Which step in the sequence for a decision comes immediately after deciding?

options.text: Gather the facts
Record the reasoning
Define the decision
Identify the risks

questions.prompt: Why is it still a sound decision if the customer's payment is delayed?

options.text: A delay to a payment is always acceptable in the Civil Service
The customer ought to have signed the form, so the outcome is his fault
The reasoning rested on the rules and risks, even though the outcome was unwelcome
Outcomes are never considered by assessors, who look only at how quickly a decision was taken

questions.hint: A good decision is judged on reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes the risk of waiting in this example?

options.text: The payment may be late, which affects the customer
The form may fade or become illegible while it is held
The team leader may be annoyed at being asked
The cut-off date may be moved without notice

questions.hint: The cost of delay is a risk of waiting.

questions.prompt: 'I left it for my manager.' What is missing from this Making Effective Decisions answer?

options.text: The name of the manager she referred it to
A date by which the decision was made
Any weighing of options before referring it
An apology to the customer for the delay

questions.hint: Escalation without weighing is not a decision.

questions.prompt: Which question should be answered first?

options.text: What will my manager think of me if I get it wrong?
How soon can I finish this and move on to other work?
Which colleague is the most senior in the room?
What exactly is the decision I need to make?

questions.prompt: Which piece of evidence best shows regard for the rules?

options.text: She followed the same approach as a colleague did last month
She decided on the basis of what seemed fair to the customer
She checked the guidance before choosing
She asked the customer what he preferred

questions.hint: Looking up the guidance is the evidence.

questions.prompt: Why record the reason for a decision?

options.text: To make the case file longer, so that it looks complete when audited
To protect the customer's feelings about the outcome
So others can understand and check the decision later
Because the manager may have forgotten the guidance

questions.prompt: In which situation is asking for advice before deciding most appropriate?

options.text: When the decision is only about the order of your own tasks
When the answer is already printed clearly on the form and the rule is not in doubt
When no customer is affected by the outcome at all
When the guidance is unclear and the choice affects someone's entitlement

questions.hint: Seeking advice fits uncertain, higher-risk choices.

items.title: L7: Handling a complaint as evidence
items.source: Civil Service Code and GOV.UK service guidance
items.body: A complaint story can be strong evidence for Managing a Quality Service and Communicating and Influencing, but only if the candidate shows a sequence of good steps. A typical effective sequence runs as follows. Listen without interrupting and make sure you understand the problem. Show that you have heard the person, for example by summarising it. Check the facts and the relevant rules. Explain what can and cannot be done in plain language. Put right what you can. Refer what you cannot to the correct person, with a clear handover so the customer does not have to repeat themselves. Follow up to confirm the outcome. Record what happened so the pattern can be seen. Many candidates fail to include the final two steps. A good answer might read: 'A customer called because a letter said her payment was stopped. I listened, summarised what she had said, checked her record and found a keying error on our side. I corrected it, explained what had happened and when she would be paid, and phoned the following day to check the payment had arrived. I logged the cause so the team could check for similar cases.' Notice the apology is for the error, not an admission that every complaint is valid. Public bodies often have formal complaint procedures, so knowing when to pass a complaint on is part of good service. Do not argue, make promises you cannot keep or blame colleagues in front of the customer.

questions.prompt: Which step is most often missing from candidates' complaint stories?

options.text: Listening
Greeting the customer
Using the customer's name
Follow-up and recording

questions.hint: The final steps are often left out.

questions.prompt: Why summarise the customer's problem back to her?

options.text: It lengthens the call so that the target time is met
It shows she has been heard and checks understanding
It lets the officer avoid acting until the facts are clear
It protects the department from legal action later

questions.prompt: Which response is least appropriate when a customer complains about something outside your authority?

options.text: Explaining what you can do
Promising an outcome you cannot guarantee
Referring her to the right person with a clear handover
Recording the complaint

questions.hint: Do not make promises you cannot keep.

questions.prompt: What does a clear handover achieve?

options.text: The officer is no longer responsible for the complaint
The complaint is automatically closed on the system
The customer does not have to repeat the story
The colleague does not need to check the facts again

questions.prompt: Why log the cause of the error in the example?

options.text: To confirm the payment arrived
To satisfy the customer's request for a call back
To avoid being phoned by her again that week
To make the call log look complete

questions.prompt: In the example, why did the officer phone the next day?

options.text: To apologise a second time
To confirm the payment arrived
To ask for feedback on her tone
To close the call log

questions.prompt: Which behaviour is wrong when handling a complaint?

options.text: Blaming a colleague in front of the customer
Checking the record before replying
Explaining what can and cannot be done
Offering a clear timescale for the outcome

questions.prompt: Which pair of Behaviours does a good complaint story usually evidence?

options.text: Leadership and Seeing the Big Picture, because complaints are about the department's wider reputation
Changing and Improving and Delivering at Pace
Managing a Quality Service and Communicating and Influencing
Making Effective Decisions and Developing Self and Others

questions.hint: Putting things right and communicating clearly.

questions.prompt: What should the apology in a complaint answer be for?

options.text: The error or the experience the customer had
Every complaint, whether or not it was valid
The customer's mistake
The department's existence

questions.prompt: Why does knowing the complaint procedure matter?

options.text: Part of good service is knowing when to pass a complaint on
It lets the officer avoid dealing with complaints
Procedures apply only to managers, not to front-line staff
It replaces the need to listen to the customer

questions.hint: Referral to the right route is part of service.

items.title: L7: Working Together when colleagues disagree
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Working Together is not the same as always agreeing. It is about building trust and helping a group to achieve a shared goal, and that sometimes means dealing with disagreement. A strong disagreement story follows a pattern. The person recognises the disagreement early, rather than letting it grow. She tries to understand the other view by asking questions and restating it. She finds the shared goal that both sides care about, such as getting claims processed accurately or keeping a rota fair. She suggests options that meet the goal, and the group agrees one. She checks later that the arrangement is working. Avoidance, such as staying silent to keep the peace, or winning an argument by pulling rank, are not good evidence. Consider two colleagues who disagree about who covers the late shift. A volunteer notices the tension, asks each privately what the problem is, and learns that one has childcare on Tuesdays and the other has a course on Thursdays. She proposes a swap which suits both, checks both agree, and reviews it two weeks later. That is strong evidence. In contrast, 'I told them to stop arguing' shows little. A story in which she complained to the manager is not necessarily bad, but it needs to show that she first tried to resolve it where appropriate and went to the manager for a good reason. Respect and inclusion matter, so avoid describing colleagues in disparaging terms. The Civil Service values fair treatment and respect for others.

questions.prompt: Which opening step in a disagreement story shows Working Together best?

options.text: Asking each colleague privately what the problem is
Telling them both firmly to stop arguing
Waiting to see which of them gives in first
Reporting them to the manager straight away

questions.prompt: In the late-shift example, what was the shared goal?

options.text: Proving which colleague was right
Reducing the number of staff on the rota
Making sure the late shift was covered fairly
Avoiding the manager's involvement

questions.hint: The shared goal is the basis for agreement.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour is poor evidence of Working Together?

options.text: Restating the other person's view back to them
Suggesting options that meet the shared goal
Reviewing the arrangement a fortnight later
Staying silent to keep the peace while the problem grows

questions.prompt: Why does the volunteer review the swap two weeks later?

options.text: To show that she had been right about the swap all along
To report the colleagues if either has slipped
To check that the solution is still working for everyone
To change the rota again whatever the result

questions.prompt: 'I told them to stop arguing.' Why is this weak?

options.text: It is rude, and rudeness is always marked down
It shows no understanding of the cause or of a solution
It is too short to count as an Action
It does not name either of the colleagues involved

questions.hint: Telling people to stop does not resolve it.

questions.prompt: When is going to a manager a reasonable part of a disagreement story?

options.text: When resolution has been tried where appropriate, or the matter needs authority
Always, as the first step, because managers are paid to settle disagreements between staff
Never, because going to a manager shows weakness
Only if the other person is more senior than you

questions.prompt: Which description of a colleague would damage an answer?

options.text: 'He had a different view of the priorities.'
'He is lazy and difficult to work with.'
'We saw the rota differently.'
'She had a course on Thursdays.'

questions.prompt: What does 'restating' the other person's view achieve?

options.text: It proves that you agree with the other person
It ends the discussion so that a decision can be made
It shifts the blame onto the other person
It checks you have understood and shows respect

questions.prompt: Why might pulling rank be poor evidence of Working Together?

options.text: It is not permitted under Civil Service rules
It is always dishonest in an application
It shows too much confidence for an entry-level role
It wins the argument without building trust

questions.hint: Trust is the aim of the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which value in the Civil Service Code is closest to fair treatment of colleagues in a disagreement?

options.text: Impartiality
Efficiency
Competitiveness
Ambition

items.title: L7: Changing and Improving when others resist
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Many Changing and Improving answers ignore the hard part: other people are often wary of change. A realistic story shows how the candidate dealt with that. A structured approach is to understand why people are reluctant, start small, show evidence, and adjust. Reasons for resistance often include worry about extra work, doubt that the new way is better and habit. Consider an officer who proposes that a colour-coded tray replaces a shared notebook for urgent cases. Colleagues say the notebook works fine. She asks what they would need to see to be convinced, runs a two-week trial with her own work only, counts how many urgent cases were missed under each approach, and shows the results. Two colleagues try it, suggest a labelling change which she adopts, and the team agrees to adopt it. This story has what assessors look for: a problem, an idea, consultation, a test, evidence, adjustment following feedback and adoption. Compare 'I suggested a better system and people liked it', which has no evidence, or 'I just started doing it my way', which ignores colleagues and may break procedures. Also note that an improvement can fail. A story where a trial showed the idea did not work, and the candidate stopped, shared what she learned and tried a different approach, can still score well, because it shows honest evaluation. Improvements should respect rules and security requirements, so check with a supervisor before changing a process that others rely on.

questions.prompt: What is the best first move when colleagues doubt a proposed change?

options.text: Ask what they would need to see to be convinced
Insist that the new way is better and say it again
Introduce it quietly across the whole team without telling them
Wait until the doubters have moved on to other jobs

questions.hint: Understanding the doubt guides the evidence.

questions.prompt: Why did the officer run a trial with her own work only?

options.text: It meant she did not have to tell her supervisor
It was quicker than testing it with the whole team
It tested the idea without affecting others
It would prove her colleagues wrong straight away

questions.prompt: Which element makes the tray story convincing evidence?

options.text: She felt confident that the idea would work
She counted missed urgent cases under each approach
She had a good relationship with her team already
She chose colours that were easy to tell apart

questions.prompt: Why is 'I just started doing it my way' a poor improvement story?

options.text: It shows too much initiative for an entry-level role
It takes too long to describe within the word limit
It names no tools or systems that she used
It ignores colleagues and may break procedures

questions.hint: Change should be agreed where others are affected.

questions.prompt: A trial shows an idea did not work. Which response best shows Changing and Improving?

options.text: Hide the results and carry on using the idea anyway, in the hope it improves
Stop, share what was learned and try a different approach
Run the trial again unchanged for a further year
Blame colleagues who had not used it properly

questions.prompt: Why adopt a colleague's labelling change?

options.text: It shows she listens and improves the idea with others
It reduces the workload on the whole team immediately
It is required by the Civil Service Code for any change
It makes the tray look better on the desk

questions.prompt: Which reason for resistance is mentioned?

options.text: Dislike of colour
Belief the idea was too cheap
Worry about extra work
A rule against suggestions

questions.prompt: Before changing a process others rely on, what should an officer do?

options.text: Wait for a complaint
Change it at the weekend
Ask the customer
Check with a supervisor

questions.prompt: 'I suggested a better system and people liked it.' What is the problem?

options.text: It is too long to be read within the word limit
There is no evidence of what changed or by how much
It uses the word 'suggested', which assessors dislike
It names a system without describing it

questions.prompt: Which sequence best matches a strong Changing and Improving story?

options.text: Idea, adoption, problem, test, evidence, adjustment, consultation
Problem, idea, consultation, test, evidence, adjustment, adoption

items.title: L7: Delivering at Pace with competing demands
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A pace story becomes much stronger when the candidate faces competing demands, not just one large task. Competing demands test prioritising, honest communication and judgement about what must give. A practical way to prioritise is to ask two questions of each task: how urgent is it, and what is the consequence if it is late or wrong? A task due today with a serious consequence goes first; a task due next week with a minor consequence goes later. Tasks can also be broken down into stages, with the most time-critical stage done first. Consider a clerk with three jobs on Thursday: a payment batch due to leave at noon, a set of letters due Friday, and an enquiry from a manager who wants figures 'when you can'. She does the batch first, arranges with a colleague to prepare the letters, and tells the manager she can send figures by Friday morning. This shows planning, delegation within agreed roles and communication about what will be late. If everything cannot be done, the correct move is to tell someone early, with options, rather than quietly miss a deadline. Hiding a problem until the deadline passes is poor evidence. Equally, taking on everything and working until late every night may show commitment but not good planning. Assessors want to see a sustainable approach: realistic estimates, early warnings and a review of what worked afterwards. Where a plan changes, say what changed and why.

questions.prompt: Which two questions form the practical prioritising test mentioned?

options.text: How long will it take to do, and who is the person that asked for it?
How urgent is it, and what is the consequence if it is late or wrong?
How easy is it, and how much do I like doing it?
How old is the request, and where is it filed?

questions.prompt: With a payment batch due at noon, letters due Friday and figures 'when you can', which should the clerk do first?

options.text: The letters
The manager's figures
The payment batch
Whichever is quickest

questions.prompt: What did the clerk do about the manager's request?

options.text: Ignored it, because it was not marked as urgent
Told him when she could realistically deliver it
Did it first to please him, then rushed the batch
Passed it to the customer to deal with

questions.prompt: If everything cannot be done in time, what is the best move?

options.text: Quietly miss the deadline
Work until the early hours and say nothing
Tell someone early and offer options

questions.prompt: Why is working late every night poor evidence of good planning?

options.text: Working late is forbidden in the Civil Service, so it can never appear in an application
It is always a sign that the candidate is being dishonest
It may show commitment but not realistic estimates or prioritising
It always reduces the quality of the work done

questions.prompt: Which breakdown of a large task best supports pace?

options.text: Splitting it into stages and doing the most time-critical stage first
Doing the easiest stage first to build momentum and make the task feel less large
Doing the stages in the alphabetical order of the file names
Leaving all stages until the day before the deadline

questions.prompt: What should a candidate say when a plan changed?

options.text: Nothing, in order to keep the story simple
That the original plan had been wrong

options.text: Strong resilience under pressure

items.title: L7: Communicating and Influencing for different audiences
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Communicating and Influencing is tested through how you choose, shape and check a message. A useful framework is to ask four questions: who is the audience, what do they already know, what do they need to do or understand, and what is the best way to reach them? The same information may need three versions. For example, a change to opening hours might need a one-line text for regular visitors, a clear poster with large print for the entrance, and a short email to partner organisations explaining the reasons. Written communication should be accurate, plain and organised, usually with the key point or request near the start. Spoken communication should include listening, and checking understanding by inviting questions or asking the person to say it back. Influencing means moving someone towards a view or action, usually by understanding what matters to them, offering evidence and being open to compromise, rather than by pressure. Take a volunteer who wants a reluctant coordinator to switch to an online booking form. She finds out he fears losing older members who do not use computers, so she suggests keeping a phone booking line and shows how many bookings were missed last month. He agrees to a trial. The strong features are tailoring, evidence and compromise. Weak evidence often says 'I can talk to anyone', or lists formats without showing any decision about why they were chosen. Avoid jargon, abbreviations the audience may not know and long blocks of text.

questions.prompt: Which pair of questions begins the four-question framework?

options.text: How long is the message, and what colour is it?
Who is the audience, and what do they already know?
Who wrote the message, and when was it written?
Who is the most senior person, and who is the most junior?

questions.hint: Audience and prior knowledge come first.

questions.prompt: The coordinator fears losing older members. What was the volunteer's best move?

options.text: Insist the online form is compulsory from the next month
Suggest keeping a phone booking line and show the missed bookings
Tell the committee about his fears and let them decide
Drop the idea altogether and return to the paper form that the older members already know

questions.hint: Addressing his concern while offering evidence.

questions.prompt: Why might one change need three versions of the same message?

options.text: Different audiences need different formats and detail
The manager asked for three versions
Three versions are required by the department's guidance
It is quicker to write three short messages than one

questions.prompt: Where should the key point or request usually appear in a written message?

options.text: At the end
In the middle
In a separate attachment
Near the start

questions.prompt: Which approach is influencing rather than pressure?

options.text: Understanding what matters to the person, then offering evidence
Repeating the request until they agree
Copying their manager into the email to add weight
Pointing out their previous mistakes to show the need

questions.hint: Influence works with the person's interests.

questions.prompt: What is a good way to check that a spoken message has been understood?

options.text: Invite questions or ask the person to say it back
Repeat the message more loudly and slowly
Move on quickly so the person does not feel tested
Ask whether the person is bored

questions.hint: Checking understanding is part of communication.

questions.prompt: Which statement is the weakest evidence of Communicating and Influencing?

options.text: 'I can talk to anyone.'
'I wrote a poster in large print and put it by the entrance.'
'I phoned older members to explain the change.'
'I asked three people to read my email before I sent it.'

questions.hint: A claim with no decision or action.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with using jargon in a message for the public?

options.text: It makes the message too short to be useful
The audience may not understand it
It makes the message less accurate
It sounds too friendly for a public body

questions.prompt: Which element is a strong feature of the booking-form story?

options.text: Tailoring to the person's concern, evidence and compromise
Persuading him by repeating the request until he agrees
Using the authority of the committee to overrule him
Avoiding his objection and not mentioning it

questions.prompt: Why might a long block of text be a poor way of communicating a change in opening hours?

options.text: Readers may miss the key point
It is too detailed for people who only need the dates

It would be unfair to the regular visitors

questions.hint: Short, structured messages are easier to act on.

items.title: L7: Evidence from study, caring and career breaks
items.body: Gaps in a work history, years of study and periods of caring can all provide evidence, but applicants often feel they need to explain or apologise for them. A better approach is to treat them as sources of examples, in the same way as paid jobs. The Experience element asks what you know and have done in paid or unpaid settings, and the Behaviours accept evidence from anywhere. For study, strong examples include organising a group project, meeting deadlines across several assignments, teaching a classmate, or improving a process, such as setting up a shared notes system. Caring examples often show Managing a Quality Service, Communicating and Influencing with professionals, Making Effective Decisions and Delivering at Pace. For a career break, name it briefly and then move on to the substance: 'During a two-year break caring for a relative I...'. Application forms and interviews generally accept a short factual explanation. Do not give excessive personal detail, especially about another person's health. Do not hide a gap by changing dates, as references and employment checks may reveal this, and it is dishonest. If an advert asks for a minimum amount of experience, check what it means. Many entry-level roles ask for none and for AO roles no previous experience of the Civil Service is needed. Where experience is required, the advert normally says whether unpaid experience counts. When in doubt, check the advert or contact the recruitment team.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate treat a career break spent caring for a relative?

options.text: Leave it out and alter the dates to hide the gap
Name it briefly, then describe what she did and achieved
Apologise for it and explain at length
Describe the relative's health in detail to show the need

questions.hint: Treat it as a source of evidence.

options.text: It is dishonest, and checks may reveal it

It makes the form too long to complete
It is allowed only for applicants at EO level

items.title: L7: Strengths questions and weak-point questions
items.body: At interview, strengths questions are quick and conversational, and some ask about your weaker points. A common version is 'What would your friends say is your biggest weakness?' or 'Which part of this job would you find hardest?'. These are not traps, but a poor answer can undermine trust. Three types of answer fail. The first is the disguised strength, such as 'I work too hard', which sounds rehearsed. The second is an alarming admission that goes straight to a core part of the role, such as telling a panel you dislike dealing with the public when the post is customer-facing. The third is a refusal to name anything. A better answer names a genuine area you are working on, explains what you do to manage it, and shows progress. For example: 'I used to take on too much myself, so now I make a short list on Monday and ask for help if I am behind by Wednesday.' This shows self-awareness and Developing Self and Others. Strengths questions also check fit: answers that show you enjoy being accurate, helping people or solving problems tend to suit AO and EO roles. Do not try to second-guess the panel. Because strengths questions come quickly, long pauses are normal, but long speeches are not. Answer in one or two sentences, add a short example if natural, and be ready for a follow-up asking why. Authentic, specific answers are easier to keep up than rehearsed ones.

questions.prompt: Which answer to 'What is your biggest weakness?' is best?

options.text: 'I work too hard, and I find it hard to switch off at the end of the day.'
'I used to take on too much myself, so now I plan on Mondays and ask for help by Wednesday if I'm behind.'
'I honestly don't think I have any weaknesses.'
'I find dealing with the public difficult.'

questions.prompt: Why does 'I work too hard' fail?

options.text: It is dishonest, because nobody can work too hard
It is too long for a strengths answer
It is a disguised strength that sounds rehearsed
It mentions work, which is not allowed in a strengths answer

questions.prompt: Why is 'I dislike dealing with the public' risky for a customer-facing role?

options.text: It is too honest
It is too modest
It contradicts the interviewers
It goes to the heart of the job

questions.hint: Admissions should not undermine the core role.

questions.prompt: Which Behaviour does the Monday-list answer also support?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture
Leadership
Making Effective Decisions
Developing Self and Others

questions.prompt: How long should most strengths answers be?

options.text: Five minutes, as for a Behaviour question
One word, to keep up the pace
One or two sentences, with a short example if natural
A full STAR story with a Result

questions.prompt: What is the problem with refusing to name any weakness?

options.text: It saves time in a short interview
It is the safest answer for an applicant
It suggests a lack of self-awareness
It answers the question fully

questions.prompt: Which statement about strengths answers is accurate?

options.text: They must match the Behaviours exactly
They should be memorised in advance
They are used only for senior roles
They are easier to keep up if they are authentic

questions.prompt: How should a candidate treat a long pause before answering a strengths question?

options.text: As normal; a short pause is fine
As a sign that the answer will fail
As a reason to ask to skip the question
As a sign that the answer needs to change

options.text: To test your knowledge of the nine Behaviours in a more relaxed way
To check the qualifications and certificates you listed on the form
To fill the interview time

options.text: Avoiding routine tasks so that every day is different
Working alone with no deadlines
Persuading large groups of people
Checking details until they are right

items.title: L7: Staying consistent between application and interview
items.body: Interviewers often have your application in front of them, and follow-up questions are designed to check whether you really did what you described. Consistency between what you wrote and what you say matters for honesty and for scoring. Prepare by rereading your application before the interview and noting the key details of each story: dates, numbers, who was involved and what you personally did. If the application says you 'led a team of six', be ready to explain what leading meant, how the team was chosen and what you would do differently. Expect typical follow-ups: What was your role compared with the others? What did you say to them? What was the hardest part? What would you do differently? Answers should match the written version, but you can add detail. If you realise that something in the application was imprecise, correct it calmly at interview, saying what is accurate and why. This is better than being found out. Do not memorise the application word for word; rather know the story. Also be ready to use a different example if the panel asks for one, since they may ask about a Behaviour you did not write about. Keep a list of other stories ready. Exaggerated claims, such as inflating the number of people or the figures, can lead to difficult questions and, if false information is found, can lead to withdrawal of an offer. Honest, specific examples are easier to defend.

questions.prompt: What is the best preparation for follow-up questions?

options.text: Memorise the application word for word so that nothing differs
Reread the application and note dates, numbers, people and your own part
Ignore the application and rely on new examples
Prepare extra facts to add that are not in the application

questions.hint: Know the story, not a script.

questions.prompt: An application says the candidate 'led a team of six'. Which preparation is most useful?

options.text: Be ready to say that the team did the actual work
Change the number at interview if it feels too high
Be ready to explain what leading meant and how the team worked
Say nothing about it unless asked

questions.hint: Be able to defend the claim.

questions.prompt: What should a candidate do on realising a detail in her application was imprecise?

options.text: Hope nobody notices the difference
Change the story to match the new detail
Correct it calmly at interview and explain what is accurate
Avoid the topic if it comes up

questions.hint: Honest correction is better than being found out.

questions.prompt: Which follow-up question tests personal contribution?

options.text: 'Where did this take place, and how long did it last overall?'
'When did you finish the work, and who signed it off?'
'Who was your manager at the time, and what was their job title?'
'What was your role compared with the others?'

questions.hint: It separates your part from the group.

questions.prompt: Why keep a list of other stories ready?

options.text: The first story you wrote may turn out to be too short for the panel
It saves time in the interview because you do not need to think
The panel prefers variety, so repeated stories are scored lower
The panel may ask about a Behaviour you did not write about

questions.prompt: Why is memorising the application word for word unhelpful?

options.text: It is forbidden by the recruitment rules, which require a fresh answer
It takes too long to learn
The panel does not read the application
It sounds rehearsed and fails when questions go beyond the text

questions.hint: Knowing the story is more flexible.

questions.prompt: What may happen if false information is found in an application?

options.text: The application is simply marked down
An offer can be withdrawn
Nothing, if the interview goes well
A warning letter is sent

questions.prompt: 'What would you do differently?' is mainly testing what?

options.text: Memory of the exact events
Confidence in front of a panel
Reflection and learning
Speed of thinking on the spot

questions.prompt: Which answer to 'Can you give an exact figure?' is best if you only know roughly?

options.text: 'About thirty, though I don't have the exact number.'
'Exactly thirty-two, because I counted them all afterwards.'
'I can't remember anything about it.'
'It was a lot, so a precise figure would not help you.'

questions.prompt: Which kind of claim is hardest to defend at interview?

options.text: Specific actions that you took yourself
Honest approximations when you are unsure
Admitted mistakes and what you learned
Exaggerated numbers or responsibilities
